newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Low inflation, liberating for British unions.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Low inflation, liberating for British unions.

text.p: Low inflation, one of the proudest boasts of Britain's Conservative government, is also proving unexpectedly liberating for their traditional rivals -- trade unions.
That, at least, is the view of John Edmonds, general secretary of the GMB general union.

Edmonds, who will be at the cutting edge of a new union-government relationship if the main opposition Labour Party win a general election on May 1, says the unions will not launch huge pay claims to take advantage of what would be the first Labour government in 18 years.

"With lower inflation, the desperate pressure to keep up with price rises is not there any more as it was 20 years ago," he told Reuters. "Trade unions have in a sense been liberated from that narrow focus on pay.
"It has been a great release for us because it means we can concentrate on issues like training, job security, equal rights and promotion opportunities."
Like many trade unionists, Edmonds looks forward with guarded optimism to life under Labour which he hopes -- and opinion polls strongly suggest -- will take power in May.

He expects relations between unions and Labour to be much different from what they were in the 1960s and 1970s, when unions wielded considerable political power and many Britons believed they had the party in their pocket.
Unions will be much less political in future, concentrating instead on workplace issues. Strikes that plagued the country in the 1970s are likely to remain a thing of the past, he believes.
"People nowadays don't like strikes -- I don't think they ever did," he says.

"If there is a strike now you can be absolutely sure that there is just cause. Very, very few strikes take place because of pay. There is usually some much deeper problem which has been there for a good few years," said Edmonds, whose union is one the Britain's five largest with more than 500,000 members.
CAUTIOUS ABOUT LABOUR'S TIGHT-SPENDING PLEDGE

Edmonds is cautious when asked about shadow finance minister Gordon Brown's commitment to live within the tight public spending plans laid down by the Conservatives for the next two years and not to raise income tax rates for five years.

This angered many on the left, who felt Labour was unnecessarily limiting its ability to raise revenue to improve public services. "Brown made a very cautious and prudent statement and I can understand why he did that,"Edmonds says.

"On the other side, to match the prudence there is the commitment to spend the capital receipts from sales of council houses on a phased basis and there is the commitment to spend the windfall tax on job creation. If that happens, we will have consequent growth in the economy as well."
He was referring to Labour's only concrete tax-raising pledge -- to impose a "windfall tax" on the profits of formerly state-owned utility companies privatised by the Conservatives.

While expecting "fairness, not favours" from a Labour government, Edmonds hopes the advent of a government which is not fundamentally hostile to unions -- as unions believe the Conservatives are -- will help to improve the general climate of industrial relations.
He has no objection to Labour's plans to maintain Conservative union legislation, such as a requirement that unions must ballot members before taking strike action.
EXPECTATION TO IMPROVE WORKERS' RIGHTS

But unions do expect Labour to keep its promise to improve the rights of employees, for example by giving them a right not just to belong to a union but to be represented by one and providing greater job security for part-time workers.

They also welcome Labour's plans to introduce a national minimum wage, although Labour is unlikely to agree to the 4.26 pounds ($6.88) an hour minimum favoured by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the union umbrella organisation.
"Two big issues for us are training and investment -- we will not do well as a competitive industrial nation unless we invest a great deal more in training," Edmonds said.
He believes the government may have to put pressure on companies by making them pay a "training levy" if they do not provide adequate training to improve the skills of their staff.

But this would be a last resort for companies which failed to choose from a "menu" of training initiatives, such as giving employees "individual learning accounts" or improving apprenticeship schemes.
"The Labour party is reluctant to move into compulsion and I understand that. But the voluntary system has failed.
"We are not using our talent properly and both companies and the economy are underperforming as a result. It is disgraceful at a social level and economically nonsensical."
On one of the other great issues facing the next government, European monetary union, Edmonds takes a different view from the TUC.

He believes that in their scramble to meet the tough qualification criteria for joining a single currency, European Union countries are inflicting excessive pain on themselves in the form of higher unemployment and curbs on public spending.
"The convergence criteria are heavily deflationary," he says. "They need to be balanced by a commitment by the community to maintain high levels of employment."
"The TUC position is that we should grit our teeth and go in in the first phase. My own feeling is that we should work hard to postpone the timetable."
He welcomes Labour's plans to sign up to the European Social Chapter on workers' rights as a much-needed corrective to years of Conservative anti-union legislation.

"The rights of employees in Britain have been reduced very substantially. Frankly, when you make comparisons, you get to countries like the Philippines having better levels of protection, particularly for part-time workers, than we have." ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
